transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I guess… what really brings me in is that my body hasn’t felt like it’s fully mine lately. Like, I know that sounds dramatic, but it’s the best way I can explain it.

At first I was just moving constantly — pacing around my apartment all night, back and forth, making all these supper-club notes like it was the most urgent thing in the world. I couldn’t just sit down. It was like my legs had decided we were doing laps, whether I wanted to or not.

And then lately it’s flipped the other way. I feel so slowed down, like everything takes this ridiculous amount of effort. My sister even said it takes me forever just to get my shoes on, and she’s not wrong. I’ll be sitting there trying to do something simple and it’s like my body is moving through wet cement. It’s embarrassing, honestly. That’s why I’m here.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is there?

I don’t think so. I mean… not like someone talking to me in the room when nobody’s there. I haven’t noticed voices, exactly.

Sometimes when I’m really tired or worked up I’ll kind of replay conversations in my head, like hear my sister’s tone or something I should’ve said differently, but that feels like my own mind doing it, if that makes sense. Not a separate voice. Not someone telling me things. So… no, I don’t think I’ve been hearing voices.
Do you feel like an outside force is controlling your body or your movements?

I don’t think so… not like an outside force, no.

I know I said my body doesn’t feel fully mine, but I don’t mean it like someone else is moving me around or controlling my arms or legs. It’s more like I’m either wound up and can’t settle, or everything feels heavy and delayed, if that makes sense. Like my body is not cooperating with me, but I don’t have the sense that some person or force is directing it.

I guess if you’re asking whether I feel possessed or controlled or like something is making me move against my will… no, I haven’t noticed that. It feels scary, but not in that way.
Have you had a strong belief that other people would say is not true?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, at the time I wouldn’t have called it “not true,” I would’ve said everybody else just wasn’t seeing it yet.

I got really convinced that I was about to build this bilingual supper club — like, not just a little dinner thing, but the best one in the city. I had all these notes about menus and themes and how it would bring people together, and I honestly believed investors would be stupid not to back me. Like I could already picture them hearing the idea and being like, “Obviously, here’s the money.”

And the thing is… I didn’t have the money lined up. I didn’t even really have a job at that point, so looking back, it sounds kind of ridiculous to say I was thinking in terms of investors and citywide buzz and all that. But I really believed it. It didn’t feel like a fantasy then. It felt obvious, like I was just ahead of everyone else.
Have you had times when that strong belief about the supper club continued even when your mood felt normal?

No, I don’t think so. It was really tied to that elevated, charged-up state I was in.

Like when I was in it, the supper club idea felt completely obvious to me — not just “I’d like to try this someday,” but like, “I’m about to make the best bilingual supper club in the city, and anyone with money would be dumb not to invest.” And looking back, that’s the part that feels embarrassing, because I didn’t have a job then, I didn’t have money lined up, I didn’t have any real plan beyond all these intense notes and ideas.

When my mood felt more normal, I could still think, “Okay, maybe it’s a cool idea,” but I wasn’t walking around with that same certainty that it was basically guaranteed or that investors would just automatically see my brilliance or whatever. That huge confidence — that feeling like I was ahead of everyone and they just needed to catch up — that seemed to come with the mood, not outside of it.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah… definitely more than two weeks. It’s been, honestly, around three months now where that heavy, slowed-down feeling has been there most of the time.

It’s not like one bad weekend or a rough few days where I can shake it off. It’s been kind of sitting on me day after day, like I wake up and it’s already there. I keep thinking maybe it’ll lift, or maybe I’m just tired, but then another week goes by and it’s still the same general weight. So yes, if you’re asking whether it’s been at least two weeks, then yeah — it’s been much longer than that.
During this three-month depressed period, have you had any beliefs that other people said were definitely not true?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think.

During these last three months, it’s been more like I’ve felt really low and stuck in my head, but I haven’t had that same kind of “I know something everyone else doesn’t” feeling. Like with the supper club thing, people probably could’ve said, “That’s not realistic,” and I would’ve argued with them. But in this depressed stretch, I can’t think of a belief like that — something where someone close to me was saying, “No, that is definitely not true,” and I kept insisting on it anyway.

I mean, I’ve had negative thoughts, for sure, but if you mean a strong belief that was clearly false to other people… no, I haven’t really noticed that.
During that charged-up period, did you ever see things that other people could not see?

I don’t think so… I mean, not literally seeing things, if that’s what you mean.

During that charged-up time, my mind was definitely moving really fast, and I was interpreting everything like it mattered or like it was pointing toward this supper club idea being some huge thing. But I don’t remember seeing a person or an object or something in the room that other people couldn’t see. It was more like my thoughts and my confidence were way out ahead of reality, not like there were visual things appearing.

I guess I want to be careful because that whole period feels kind of intense and embarrassing to look back on, but no — I can’t think of a time where someone else was like, “There’s nothing there,” and I was seeing it anyway.
During that charged-up period, were you hospitalized because of it?

I’m not sure how to answer that, because I don’t think I should say yes if I don’t have that information straight.

I don’t remember being hospitalized for it, at least not in the sense of being admitted somewhere and staying there because of that charged-up period. There were definitely people who were worried about me, and looking back it felt like things got really out of hand in my head, but if you mean formally hospitalized — like taken to a hospital or kept on a unit — I don’t think that happened.

I guess I’m hesitating because that whole time is a little blurry in parts, and I don’t want to accidentally make it sound more exact than it is. But as far as I know, no, I wasn’t hospitalized because of it.
During that charged-up period, did your behavior cause serious problems in your life?

Yeah… yes, it did. I don’t really like admitting that, because at the time I would’ve said I was just “busy” or “building something” or that other people didn’t understand what I was trying to do, but looking back, it caused real problems.

I wasn’t keeping things together. Work was a mess — like I couldn’t follow through on plans or keep my schedule straight the way I normally would. Rent stuff got disorganized too, and I remember arrangements around money and where I was supposed to be staying just becoming this tangled thing I kept saying I’d handle, but I wasn’t actually handling it. And family commitments… I was dropping those or making promises and then not doing them, or turning everything into part of my big plan instead of just doing the basic thing I’d agreed to do.

It got bad enough that my sister had to take me to a crisis clinic. That’s probably the clearest sign, honestly. I couldn’t get basic responsibilities organized on my own by then. I was still talking like I had everything under control, but I really didn’t. So yes, it caused serious problems — not just people being annoyed with me, but actual life stuff falling apart.
During that charged-up period, did you believe you had special powers, a special identity, or an unusually important mission?

Yeah… I mean, I didn’t think I had, like, supernatural powers or anything like that. But I did believe I was on the edge of something unusually important.

At the time I honestly believed I was about to build the best bilingual supper club in the city. Not just a nice little restaurant idea or a pop-up — I mean I really thought it was going to be the thing everyone would recognize as brilliant once they heard it. I was talking about it like it was obvious, like investors would be stupid not to back me. And that’s embarrassing to say now because I didn’t even have the money lined up, and I didn’t have a job at that point, so it wasn’t exactly grounded in reality.

But in my head, it felt clear. Like I had this special angle, this mission almost, to bring people together through food and language and culture, and I thought I was the one who could see it when other people couldn’t. If someone questioned it, I took it like they just didn’t understand the scale of what I was doing. So yes, not “special powers,” but definitely an inflated sense that I had this big important thing I was destined to pull off.
During that charged-up period, did you ever feel especially important in a way that other people said was not true?

Yeah… I did. I mean, I wouldn’t have used those words at the time — “especially important” sounds so blunt — but that’s basically what it was.

I really believed I was about to create the best bilingual supper club in the city. Like, not just a fun idea or something I could maybe try if I got my life together. I thought it was obvious that it was going to be big, and that I was the person who saw it clearly before everyone else did. If people pushed back or asked practical questions, I felt like they were being small-minded, honestly.

And I remember thinking investors would be stupid not to back me, which sounds ridiculous now because I didn’t even have a job then, and I didn’t have the money lined up. But at the time, that didn’t feel like a real obstacle. It felt like once people heard me explain it, they’d see how important it was. So yes, other people were telling me it wasn’t realistic, or not on the scale I was making it out to be, and I just thought they didn’t get it.

But in my head, it felt clear. Like I had this special angle, this mission almost, to bring people together through food and language and culture, and I thought I was the one who could see it when other people couldn’t. If someone questioned it, I took it like they just didn’t understand the scale of what I was doing. So yes, not “special powers,” but definitely an inflated sense that I had this big important thing I was destined to pull off.

Yeah… I did. I mean, I wouldn’t have used those words at the time — “especially important” sounds so blunt — but that’s basically what it was.

I really believed I was about to create the best bilingual supper club in the city. Like, not just a fun idea or something I could maybe try if I got my life together. And I remember thinking investors would be stupid not to back me, which sounds ridiculous now because I didn’t even have a job then, and I didn’t have the money lined up.
